_comment: Topic lexicons for scripts/build_topic_index.py. Patterns are case-insensitive regular expressions matched against a variable's question text. They are phrase-led on purpose: a bare word list picks up 'free and fair elections' for fairness, 'overcrowded classrooms' for class and 'poor teaching' for poverty. Every pattern here was written after reading what it matches. Edit and re-run to change what the index counts.

inequality.title: Inequality
inequality.description: Questions about unequal outcomes, unequal treatment and unequal access, across every survey in the archive.

figures.title: Conditions and perception
figures.caption: Region by region, what people go without against whether they say equality is applied. The two axes come from different programmes and different respondents, and rank the seven regions almost identically (ρ = −0.89); the relationship is re-run across governorates within one programme, where it is weaker but holds.

figures.title: What people go without
figures.caption: Afrobarometer's Lived Poverty Index — how often a household went without food, clean water, medical care, cooking fuel or cash income — by region across six rounds, 2013 to 2024.

figures.title: What is in the place
figures.caption: Whether the enumeration area has piped water, a sewage system, a clinic, a bank, a paved road, recorded by the interviewer rather than reported by the respondent. The archive's only non-attitudinal measure of spatial inequality.

figures.title: Hardship by governorate
figures.caption: Share saying household income does not cover the household, by governorate — the finest geography the archive supports for a material measure.

figures.title: What the archive holds
figures.caption: Every inequality variable in the archive by facet and by survey, in fieldwork order — not only the ones that recur. Coverage is uneven enough that the facet decides which programme you can use.

figures.title: What can be followed over time
figures.caption: Every inequality question asked in more than two surveys, and the years it was asked in. A run of dots in one colour is a series that can be built.

figures.title: How it moved
figures.caption: The share saying equality is applied, on one common baseline, with the rest of each question's battery drawn behind it in grey.

figures.title: How Tunisians answered
figures.caption: How Tunisians answered the recurring questions, as weighted shares of substantive answers. Bars diverge from zero rather than stacking to 100%, so each pole keeps a common baseline; each panel carries its own scale, because the releases do not share one.

figures.title: Which kinds of equality
figures.caption: The share saying equality is applied, by the dimension asked about, pooled over eight Arab Opinion Index rounds with 95% intervals. Equality is reported to hold across the lines people are born on and to fail across the lines of money and power.

figures.title: Where
figures.caption: The same, by Tunisia's seven statistical regions. The Centre West — the poorest region, and where the 2010 uprising began — is lowest, though poverty does not order the rest.

figures.title: Who
figures.caption: The same, by household income, education, age and sex. Only household income orders people cleanly; sex does not separate them at all.

figures.title: Is it one attitude, or several?
figures.caption: Spearman rank correlations among the 25 inequality items of the survey that can support the most comparisons, grouped by battery. Within one survey only — other surveys are other people.

economic-gap.title: Economic gap and redistribution
patterns: gap between the rich and the poor

equality-principle.title: Equality as a principle
patterns: all people have the same rights

spatial.title: Spatial and regional inequality
patterns: availability of Equality of all citizens regardless of their geographic

excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.fair: free and fair elections, fair count of votes, fair coverage, fair punishment — electoral and judicial fairness, not distributive
excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.poor: poor teaching, poor services, poor condition of facilities — quality, not poverty
excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.region: province or region sampling variables, and regional organisations such as the Arab Maghreb Union
excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.tax: tax compliance and tax authority questions, which are about the state's reach rather than redistribution
excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.living conditions compared: 'your living conditions compared to 12 months ago' is a change over time, not a gap between people; only the relational form is matched

_facet_notes.lived-poverty: Afrobarometer's five-item Lived Poverty Index and the World Values Survey's shorter version: how often a household went without food, water, medical care, cooking fuel or cash income. Experienced deprivation, not an opinion about inequality — the only measure here of what people actually lack.
_facet_notes.spatial: Two different things, deliberately together. The Arab Opinion Index and Afrobarometer each ask one question about equality across regions. The rest are Afrobarometer's enumeration-area checklist (EA-SVC, EA-FAC, EA-ROAD), which the interviewer records on arrival: whether the place has piped water, a sewage system, a clinic, a bank, a paved road. Those are observations of a place rather than answers from a respondent, and are the archive's only non-attitudinal measure of spatial inequality.

regime-preference.title: Regime preference
regime-preference.description: What kind of political system people say they want, and what they say about the alternatives. Preference is kept apart from two things it is easily confused with: how democratic people judge their own country to be, and how democratic they rate other countries. Both are assessments, both have their own facet, and neither is a preference.

preferred-system.title: Which system is preferred
patterns: preferable for (the system of governance|[a-z]+ to have)
which of the following political systems
most suitable to be the system of government
how appropriate each of these would be for your country
mention some of the political systems

non-democratic-alternatives.title: Support for non-democratic alternatives
patterns: does not have to bother with parliament

democracy-support.title: Support for democracy against its drawbacks
patterns: democratic systems? (may have problems|are not effective|is not effective)
non-democratic systems? (may have problems|are not effective)

suitability-readiness.title: Whether democracy suits the country
patterns: extent to which democracy is suitable
not prepared for a democratic system

religion-and-rule.title: Religion and the basis of rule
patterns: laws of your country match the sharia
governed by religious law vs secular

regime-assessment.title: How democratic the country is judged to be (assessment, not preference)
patterns: level of democracy:? (today|ten years ago|in the future|under previous)
measuring the extent to which your country is democratic

external-models.title: How democratic other countries are rated (a model, not this country)
patterns: rate the level of democracy in

excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.army: trust in the army, armed forces as an institution, and soldiers or roadblocks recorded in the sampling unit — only army rule is a regime preference
excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.regime: 'the fall of the Asad regime', satisfaction with the Mubarak regime — a named government, not a preference over regime types
excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.rule of law: the state's application of the rule of law between citizens, which is governance quality
excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.political system (trust): trust in political institutions, which is support for incumbents rather than for a system
excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.level of democracy (elsewhere): Afrobarometer Round 5 and the Arab Opinion Index 2011 rate how democratic China, the USA, France, Iran, Turkey, Israel and Saudi Arabia are; those are ratings of other countries and sit in their own facet rather than in this country's assessment

democracy-perception.title: Perception of democracy
democracy-perception.description: How Tunisians judge and rate democracy — how democratic they say their country is, how satisfied they are with the way it works, what they take democracy to mean, and how free they think elections are. This is assessment, not preference: whether people want democracy is a separate question, indexed under [regime preference](regime-preference.md), which keeps its own assessment facets for the same items seen from the other side.

assessment.title: How democratic the country is judged to be

satisfaction.title: Satisfaction with the way democracy works

patterns: democracy.{0,30}(compared to|five years ago|in five years)

meaning.title: What democracy is taken to mean

elections.title: Whether elections are judged free and fair

benchmark.title: How democratic other countries are judged to be (a yardstick, not this country)

suitability.title: Whether democracy is judged to fit the country
patterns: extent to which democracy is suit

excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.democratic party: party names containing 'Democratic' are organisations, not judgements
excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.democracy as a preference: wanting democracy is regime preference; this topic is about how people rate what they have
excluded_because_they_are_false_friends.scale measuring the level of democracy: the shared preamble of Arab Barometer's rating battery, repeated on the item for every country it asks about — it matched the Iran item as though it were about Tunisia

figures.title: Testing 'Tunisians fear democracy'
figures.caption: The claim tested on its own terms, four ways, across three programmes and 17 surveys. Support for democracy in principle never collapses; what fell is confidence that democracy is decisive, and disapproval of one-man rule — the latter by 2020, before the coup. Draws on items indexed under both this topic and regime preference.

figures.title: Before and after the self-coup
figures.caption: How democratic Tunisians say their country is, and how satisfied they are with the way it works, across six Afrobarometer rounds. Round 8 was fielded 17 months before 25 July 2021 and Round 9 seven months after; both readings fall sharply across that break and then exceed their pre-coup levels by 2024.

figures.title: What each programme says
figures.caption: Every reading the archive holds on how democratic Tunisia is, from three programmes that ask it three different ways — drawn apart rather than joined, with the one same-year check reported whichever way it comes out.

figures.title: Whether the swing was general
figures.caption: The share calling Tunisia a democracy, by region and by urban or rural residence, in the round before the self-coup and the two after.

figures.title: What the word is taken to mean
figures.caption: What Tunisians picked as most essential to democracy in 2013: delivery ranks far above procedural liberty, which bears on how a later rating should be read.
